title: The Most Important End-of-Year Task
author: Regenerative Schools
summary: Using sandhill cranes' migratory cycles as a metaphor, Regenerative Schools argues that June reflection is the most important end-of-year task an educator or school leader can perform -- and the one they should never cut even when everything else is being pruned. The article provides a structured reflection protocol -- Toss, Tweak, Treasure -- from the Institute for Social and Emotional Learning, along with specific prompt categories for school leaders: pruning the task list, building buffers for thinking, culture of well-being, trust-building, collaboration, and culture of agency. It then argues for vulnerable transparency: sharing some of what you discovered in reflection with your team. Leaders who model hard work and rest, reflection and transparency, build regenerative schools that can sustain improvement across cycles.
points: June reflection is the most important gift a school leader can give their future self: like cranes completing a migratory cycle, the annual rhythm of intense effort followed by reflective rest enables sustainable renewal rather than accumulated depletion.

The Toss/Tweak/Treasure protocol provides a simple but powerful reflection structure: what to cut (didn't go well), what to change (needs adjustment), and what to preserve (went well enough to repeat intentionally).
The power of structured reflection prompts lies not in specific questions but in the process of thinking deeply and recording thoughts before the summer erases the year's hard-won learning.

Leaders who share reflections vulnerably with their team -- 'what went well as a leader, what I want to do differently' -- model the same courageous behaviors they ask teachers to demonstrate in classrooms and evaluations.

Regenerative leadership is cyclical, not linear: attuning to the year's rhythms, modeling hard work and rest, and practicing reflection alongside transparency are the specific behaviors that build schools capable of sustaining improvement.
quotes: One of the great joys of being an educator is our own cyclical rhythm of the school year. Like the cranes, we have an annual journey of hard work, of intense effort, of striving together with our community, and then the great exhale of reaching our destination.

Though I often advocate that regenerative educators prune as many tasks from your list as you can during the hectic end of year season, reflection is the one task I would never ever cut. June reflection is probably the most important gift you can give your future self.
We do not learn from experience. We learn from reflecting on experience.
The specific questions are not where the power lies: the power lies in the process of thinking deeply, and then recording our thoughts so we don't forget them in the luxurious rest of summer break.

Although this kind of transparency can feel really vulnerable, regenerative leadership is courageous! We ask teachers to do vulnerable things all the time, like trying something new or being evaluated.
Leaders who are attuned to the cycles of the year, who model hard work and rest, reflection and transparency: these are the leaders who build regenerative schools." Page 1
